Let the third-column entries, in increasing order, be  
\[
c_1<c_2<\cdots<c_6.
\]
For the \(j\) smallest such entries, each row needs two smaller numbers, giving \(2j\) numbers below \(c_j\). Also, the \(j-1\) smaller third-column entries \(c_1,\dots,c_{j-1}\) are below \(c_j\). Thus
\[
c_j-1 \ge 2j+(j-1)=3j-1,
\]
so
\[
c_j\ge 3j.
\]
Therefore the sum is at least
\[
3+6+9+12+15+18=63.
\]

This is achievable, for example:
\[
\begin{array}{cccccc}
1&2&3&19&20&21\\
4&5&6&22&23&24\\
7&8&9&25&26&27\\
10&11&12&28&29&30\\
13&14&15&31&32&33\\
16&17&18&34&35&36
\end{array}
\]
The third-column sum is \(3+6+9+12+15+18=63\).

\[
\boxed{63}
\]
